name: Mohamed Rashidh
about_me: I own AI systems and the platforms behind them, end to end, from architecture to production. I've designed and deployed two production AI agents for an Abu Dhabi government entity, architected the multi-tenant commerce and ERP backend a group of companies runs on, and built the fast, search-ready websites in front of it. I take a business problem, decide the architecture, build it, integrate it with the systems the organization already runs (ERP, commerce, telephony, email) and keep it reliable in production. First-class B.Sc. (Hons) in Computer Science & Software Engineering, University of Bedfordshire.

principles.title: Own the architecture, not just the ticket
principles.detail: I decide how a system is built, not just implement someone else's spec — from the government agents' failover design to the commerce platform's ERP backbone.

principles.title: Ground every answer in real data
principles.detail: The AI agent on this page answers strictly from my real profile — the same discipline I build into every production agent: no invented facts.

principles.title: Design for provider failure, not just success
principles.detail: Multi-provider failover and reliability engineering aren't an afterthought — a government-facing agent can't go down because one model API had an outage.

principles.title: Integrate with what already exists
principles.detail: ERP, commerce, telephony, email — I build AI that plugs into the systems an organization already runs, not a parallel system nobody adopts.

case_studies.title: Production AI Agents for an Abu Dhabi Government Entity
case_studies.problem: A government entity needed two AI agents that could answer from its own, frequently-updated documents and stay available even when a model provider had an outage — downtime wasn't an option for a government-facing service.
approach: Each agent runs on a RAG knowledge base that re-indexes updated source documents automatically, so answers stay current without a manual redeploy or someone re-uploading files by hand.

Behind both agents sits a multi-LLM orchestration layer I architected — one API in front of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and other providers, with model switching, fallback handling, centralised tool execution and message compaction.
Real-time response streaming runs over Redis pub/sub with caching, so duplicate model calls don't pile up and response latency stays flat under concurrent load.

decisions.title: Multi-provider failover over a single vendor
decisions.detail: A government service can't go down because one model provider has an outage. Routing through an orchestration layer with automatic fallback kept the agents answering even when a single upstream provider didn't.

decisions.title: Auto re-indexing over manual updates
decisions.detail: Government documents change on their own schedule, not the engineering team's. Automatic re-indexing meant accuracy didn't depend on someone remembering to update the knowledge base.

decisions.title: Message compaction over a bigger context window
decisions.detail: Rather than leaning on ever-larger context windows, compacting conversation history removed context-overflow errors outright and lowered token costs per conversation.

case_studies.outcome: Two agents in production, serving a government entity continuously, with RAG knowledge bases that update themselves and a provider-failure story that doesn't require paging anyone.

case_studies.title: One Backend for a Group of Companies
case_studies.problem: The group runs several companies, each with its own website, products, prices, payment methods, couriers and company in Odoo ERP. They needed one platform all of them could share, without any company ever being able to see another's data.
approach: I designed and built a multi-tenant backend in NestJS 11 and TypeScript. Each company is a store, isolated in the database itself with PostgreSQL 17 Row-Level Security. 40 domain modules (catalog, inventory, orders, payments, invoicing, loyalty, reviews, SEO, reporting and more) expose 590+ documented API operations over 155 tables.

Staff sign in through Keycloak with per-store roles and permissions. A separate worker runs BullMQ jobs, and a transactional outbox writes every event in the same database transaction as the change it describes, so nothing is lost between a sale and the systems that need to hear about it.

Payments, couriers and messaging sit behind contracts with swappable providers: Stripe, Tabby, Tamara, Razorpay, Moyasar and cash on delivery; SMSA, Shipa, Delhivery and 17TRACK; email, SMS and WhatsApp. Confirmed orders route to the right Odoo company on their own, and an Odoo add-on I wrote sends deliveries, tracking numbers and invoices back as signed webhooks.
Around it I built an Astro and React staff dashboard: a server-side BFF that holds the login, so tokens never reach the browser.

decisions.title: Isolation in the database, not only in code
decisions.detail: Row-Level Security and separate Postgres roles for the app, background jobs and migrations (never the superuser) mean a missing filter in application code still can't leak one company's data to another.

decisions.title: An outbox, not fire-and-forget events
decisions.detail: Events are written in the business transaction and relayed by a worker, so a crash between saving an order and notifying the ERP can't drop the update.

decisions.title: Protect the ERP from the shop
decisions.detail: Pushes to Odoo are idempotent jobs: one at a time per database, rate-capped, with cached lookups so an order costs about four calls, and a circuit breaker. A shopper's order is never blocked because the ERP is down.

case_studies.outcome: One codebase built to serve every company in the group, guarded by 320 test files and released through development, staging and production stages. I'm its main author, with 460+ commits in the backend since September 2026, and I wrote the standard every company website follows when it reads from it.

case_studies.title: Running Production: Docker, Caddy and Cloudflare
case_studies.problem: A backend, a staff dashboard and six company websites had to run reliably for real customers and real payments, released often, by a small team, without a release ever taking a site down or a server holding secrets it didn't need.
approach: Two identical environments, staging and production, each split into a data server (PostgreSQL 17, Redis 7) and an apps server. They share only a private network. The data server's firewall, set in Docker's own DOCKER-USER chain, accepts database traffic from its apps server alone; from the internet it is reachable over SSH only.

Production's apps server runs 13 Docker services from one Compose file: Caddy, Keycloak, database migrations, the API and its worker, Gotenberg for PDF invoices, the staff dashboard and six websites. Caddy issues and renews HTTPS certificates for every domain, compresses responses and adds security headers, with Cloudflare in front for DNS and caching.

Each release builds a multi-stage Docker image that runs as a non-root user, scans it for vulnerabilities with Trivy, publishes it to GitHub Container Registry and deploys it over SSH. Migrations run first; if the new version isn't healthy within two minutes, the previous one starts again on its own.

Every night the databases are dumped, encrypted with age and copied off-site to Cloudflare R2 (7 daily and 4 weekly copies). Every Sunday a script restores the latest dump into a throwaway Postgres, counts stores, orders and customers, and reports the result to Telegram.

decisions.title: A deploy key that can do one thing
decisions.detail: The CI key's forced command on the server can only run the deploy script, and the registry login uses the run's own short-lived token, so no long-lived registry password is ever stored on a server.

decisions.title: Roll back without a person
decisions.detail: A health check after every deploy means a bad release undoes itself within two minutes, rather than waiting for someone to notice and act.

decisions.title: A backup only counts once it's been restored
decisions.detail: The servers hold only the public encryption key, so they can lock a backup but never open one. The weekly restore test turns "we have backups" into something checked, and a quiet week with no ✅ message means something is broken.

case_studies.outcome: Staging and production run the same way from one infrastructure repository I wrote and maintain: 13 services in production behind automatic HTTPS, releases that roll themselves back, and backups that are encrypted, off-site and tested every week.

case_studies.title: AI Inside a Commerce Operation
case_studies.problem: Every new AI idea in the business (a helpdesk, a voice line, an ERP assistant) needed someone to take it from idea to something staff and customers actually use, connected to the real order and ERP data.
approach: OdooGPT lets management query sales, stock and finance data in Odoo ERP and complete tasks in plain language, and an AI analyst web app answers management and finance questions across sales and operations data.
An MCP server lets admins make store changes by describing them, and an AI chat assistant and helpdesk handle customer-facing support.

A real-time phone voice agent answers inbound customer-service calls: a Python bridge streams call audio between Telnyx and ElevenLabs Conversational AI, with telephony providers and agents as plugins. An Odoo add-on syncs confirmed website orders to the agent every 15 minutes, so it can answer questions about a caller's order, delivery and payment.
An LLM email pipeline classifies incoming mail, drafts replies and routes requests to the right team.

decisions.title: An MCP server over a bigger admin UI
decisions.detail: Instead of building a settings screen for every new store need, exposing store actions through an MCP server lets admins describe the change they want. The interface grows with what people ask for, not with engineering time.

decisions.title: Ground the voice agent in real orders
decisions.detail: A voice agent that can't see the caller's order just transfers them. Syncing confirmed orders from Odoo lets it answer the questions people actually call about.

decisions.title: Providers as plugins
decisions.detail: The call bridge doesn't care which phone carrier or voice-AI vendor sits on either side, so switching one is a new plugin, not a rewrite.

case_studies.outcome: AI that staff and customers use every day: a live voice agent on the help desk, an ERP assistant management relies on, and email and chat support that absorb the repetitive share of requests, all reading from the same ERP as the rest of the business.

case_studies.title: Fast, Findable Websites on Astro and Cloudflare
case_studies.problem: Each brand needed a website that loads fast on a phone, ranks in search and AI answers, and lets staff change any word or picture without waiting for a developer.
approach: I wrote the website standard every company site follows, then built the sites in Astro 7: server-rendered pages, React only where something is interactive, and page copy read on the server from the backend's content store. The same words stay in the code as defaults, so a page is never empty, and staff can edit any text in place from the admin.

Everything is served through Cloudflare. Static assets are cached long-term, and store reads use a stale-while-revalidate cache with a 24-hour stale window, while reads that drive a purchase (product page, bag, checkout) always fetch fresh data. Images ship as AVIF or WebP, and the hero banner loads first instead of after the scripts.

Search and AI search are built in: structured data, sitemaps, robots.txt, llms.txt for AI crawlers, titles sized to Google's limits and Google Shopping product data, plus an accessibility pass on contrast, tap targets and labels.

For a freelance client, Emirati Tasjeel, the whole site runs on Cloudflare's free plan as one Worker: static pages, a D1 database for bookings, Turnstile spam protection, and an admin behind Cloudflare Access.

decisions.title: Stale-while-revalidate, but never at checkout
decisions.detail: A visitor after a quiet spell gets the last good page at once while it refreshes in the background. Prices and stock on the way to a purchase are always read fresh.

decisions.title: Measure, then fix the actual cause
decisions.detail: On Emirati Tasjeel, the AVIF hero took 0.7 s of phone CPU to decode. Serving it as WebP took the home page's mobile performance from 82 to 100.

decisions.title: Content in the admin, layout in code
decisions.detail: Fixed content keys mean staff can change every word and picture without a release, and the design can't be broken from the admin.

case_studies.outcome: Five live sites. Recorded mobile Lighthouse results: Emirati Tasjeel scores 100 for SEO and best practices on every page and 100 for performance on its home page; Purone and Floradyle score 100 for accessibility.
